messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elijah, a sharp and dedicated policy analyst nearing retirement at 68, found his world irrevocably altered a year ago when a sudden, crushing chest pain seized him at his home office. The memory of gasping for air, the piercing sirens, and the frantic medical team working over him in the ER remained vivid, particularly the terrifying helplessness as his own body seemed to turn against him, a betrayal that ultimately landed him in intensive care. He recovered physically, but the psychological scars ran deep, leaving him with a PCL-5 score of 77 and a pervasive sense of dread.

Now, a year later, Elijah struggles to find peace. Sometimes, when the memories surface, he can recall the sterile smells and the insistent beeping of the ICU monitors, but it feels distant, almost as if it happened to a stranger, a detached, emotionless recall. Yet, more often, a sudden tightness in his chest or the quiet hum of his refrigerator can instantly transport him back, making the memory feel like it is happening right now rather than something that is over. When these moments hit, he finds himself so overwhelmed by emotion, a suffocating wave of fear and panic, that he has to stop whatever he’s doing, unable to continue.

This constant internal battle has fundamentally changed how Elijah perceives himself and his surroundings. He has come to believe, with a chilling certainty, that he can no longer trust his own body. Every benign ache or flutter becomes a potential harbinger of another catastrophic event, reinforcing his conviction that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe. This profound sense of his body being an enemy, a treacherous vessel, feeds into a persistent state of heightened alert. He finds himself constantly tense, his muscles coiled, his senses hyper-attuned, as if his body is perpetually on guard and ready to react to danger. This vigilance follows him everywhere, even within the familiar walls of his quiet home, where he feels an unsettling sense of being on guard.

The insidious cycle continues to tighten its grip. Elijah’s deeply held belief that his body is unreliable and an enemy significantly exacerbates his chronic state of threat, making him feel constantly keyed up and watchful. This persistent state of hypervigilance, in turn, amplifies the intensity and immediacy of his traumatic memories; the slightest trigger can pull him back into the overwhelming sensation that the event is unfolding anew. The constant physiological arousal, the relentless feeling of his body on alert, further solidifies his belief that he can no longer trust himself, and he often despairs, thinking he will never be able to feel normal emotions again, trapped as he is in a perpetual state of fear.

His once-sharp focus, essential for his work as a policy analyst, has eroded. He now has difficulty concentrating, his mind often drifting to scanning his environment for threats or replaying fragments of his illness, making it nearly impossible to delve into complex reports or lead intricate discussions. The inability to relax, even in his own home, means he rarely finds respite from the internal pressure. The solitude of his widowhood, once a comfort, now feels like a prison, amplifying his sense of isolation and the terror that no one would be there if his body were to betray him again. It was this creeping despair, the feeling that his life had shrunk to merely managing his fear, that finally led Elijah to seek help, hoping to reclaim some semblance of trust in himself and his world.
